metadata.concept_name: ZeroFizz Sugar-Free Carbonated Beverage - Jobs to be Done
metadata.product_name: ZeroFizz Sugar-Free Carbonated Beverage - Jobs to be Done
metadata.objective: Understand what jobs health-conscious adults 18-35 are trying to accomplish when they reach for a sugar-free carbonated beverage — functional jobs (power through the 2pm desk slump without another coffee, substitute for a beer at a rooftop bar, scratch the soda craving without a calorie hit), emotional jobs (feel indulgent without guilt, feel alert without jittery, feel like the kind of person who reads labels), and social jobs (have an adult-coded drink in hand while friends are doing Dry January, signal wellness alignment without preaching). Probe the pains driving switching — sweetener aftertaste fatigue, a TikTok creator calling out an ingredient, price creep, availability drops at their usual grocery. Elicit desired outcomes — clean energy, recognizable short-label ingredients, a flavor that doesn't get boring. Treat Coke Zero, Celsius, LaCroix, and Olipop as category alternatives respondents are hiring against.

turns.question: I'd love to hear about your experience with drinks — especially the ones without a ton of sugar. Can you think back to a recent time when you reached for a sugar-free fizzy drink instead of something else, and walk me through what was going on that day and why that particular drink felt like the right choice?
turns.response: Yeah, so this was maybe three weeks ago — I was at my desk around mid-afternoon, hitting that energy dip, and I grabbed a ZeroFizz instead of my usual coffee. Practically speaking, it just made more sense at that point. I'd already had two coffees, didn't want the jitter, but I still needed something with a bit of kick to push through to the end of the day. The carbonation gives you that sensation without the crash, so objectively it was the logical choice. I mean, on paper it checked all the boxes — no sugar, caffeine-adjacent feeling, better than reaching for another espresso or just powering through tired. That was really the whole calculation.

turns.question: Why does making that logical, optimal choice in the moment matter to you?
turns.response: I mean, practically speaking, it just... reduces friction, right? If I'm going to grab something, I don't want to spend mental energy on whether it's the right call. I want to know it objectively checks the boxes — tastes fine, doesn't wreck my diet, doesn't cost too much. Done. But actually — and I'm realizing this as I say it — there's probably something else going on. If I'm being honest, I think it's about not feeling like I'm making a compromise. Like, if I'm choosing ZeroFizz because it *makes sense*, then I'm not settling. I'm choosing it. Not just... tolerating it because the sugar version is off-limits. Does that make sense? The logic kind of gives me permission to actually want it.

turns.question: Why does treating yourself without guilt matter more to you than just having a regular break?
turns.response: I mean, practically speaking, it's about efficiency — I don't want to feel like I'm wasting calories on something that doesn't really... satisfy me, you know? So if I'm going to take a break, it should actually do something. But, to be fair... *actually*, I think it's more that I don't want to feel like I'm making a bad choice. Like, if I grab a regular soda, there's this voice in my head going "you shouldn't be doing this," and then the break doesn't feel like a break anymore, it feels like... I don't know, sneaking around. Which is stupid when I say it out loud. With ZeroFizz I can just have the thing without that. Without that guilt sitting in the background. I suppose that's the actual part that matters — not the break itself, but being able to take it without feeling like I'm failing at something.

turns.question: Does knowing you chose ZeroFizz instead of defaulting change how you see yourself in other moments throughout your day?
turns.response: Not really, I mean... on paper it's just a beverage choice, right? I'm not someone who makes a big deal out of these things. But actually, now that you say it like that, I guess there's something about it. Like, I notice myself being a bit more intentional about other stuff — what I eat, how I move around. It's not like I suddenly became a different person or anything, but there's this weird thing where once you make one choice that feels, I don't know, deliberate instead of just defaulting, you start seeing the other defaults you've been on autopilot with. To be fair, I think I was telling myself the ZeroFizz thing was purely practical — better for my teeth, fewer calories, whatever. Which, sure, that's true. But I think what I was actually doing was giving myself permission to care a little bit. Like, if I'm going to pick something instead of just grabbing whatever, maybe I should pick other things too. It's kind of embarrassing to admit that a drink choice did that, but yeah, it sort of did.

turns.focus_node_label: feel like someone who makes deliberate, self-caring choices

turns.question: So it sounds like ZeroFizz is really about giving yourself permission to be intentional—is there anything else about that feeling that matters?
turns.response: I mean, yeah, that's... that's actually pretty accurate. Though I'd say it's less about permission and more just — practically speaking, it's about not having to make excuses, right? Like, I can have a drink that tastes good without the whole guilt spiral. But, um... to be fair, I think there's something else in there too. It's not just the logic of "fewer calories, same taste." It's that it lets me feel like I'm still... I don't know, like I'm taking care of myself while doing something I actually enjoy. Which sounds small, but it's kind of the opposite of how I used to approach it — like everything was a trade-off. Either I'm being responsible or I'm having fun. I never really thought about it that way until just now, but yeah. ZeroFizz is the thing where those don't have to be at odds anymore.
